d.title: A frame is columns that share one row index
d.caption: The index holds **labels**, not positions — and the default `RangeIndex` of `0..n-1` looks exactly like positions, which is where most of the confusion comes from. Each column is a Series with its own dtype; the values inside one column are not.

children.label: Index
children.sub: the row labels: not unique, not sorted, not positions

d.title: Three selectors, and what each one takes
d.caption: `.loc` and `.iloc` each do one thing. `[]` reads best and behaves least predictably, because what it returns depends on what you put inside it. The slice row is the one that bites: `.loc[2:5]` includes 5 and `.iloc[2:5]` does not.

d.title: Why chained indexing is a coin flip
d.caption: `df["col"][3] = 0` is two separate operations, and whether the first returns a view or a copy depends on the frame's internal block layout — which you neither control nor can see. The warning is pandas telling you it cannot promise what your assignment did.

d.title: memory_usage lies by default
d.caption: An `object` column stores 8-byte pointers, and the default report counts only those — ignoring the 50+ byte string each one leads to. On a text-heavy frame the real figure is routinely ten times what the default prints, which is why `deep=True` is the only number worth quoting.

d.title: Four ways to be missing, and only one test for all of them
d.caption: `np.nan` is a float, so a single missing value forces an integer column to float. `pd.NA` propagates through comparisons instead of returning `False`, which is the behaviour you want and the one that breaks code written for `NaN`. `isna()` is the only test that recognises all four.

d.title: How a missing value moves through an operation
d.caption: The inconsistency is deliberate and it is still a trap: arithmetic propagates, comparison returns `False`, and reductions skip. A `NaN` that vanishes from a `mean()` is the same `NaN` that silently shrinks the denominator.
cells: len minus count is the gap

d.title: pivot_table aggregates whether or not you asked it to
d.caption: `pivot_table` is `groupby` followed by `unstack`, and its default `aggfunc` is `mean` — right for a price, wrong for anything additive. It applies even when there were no duplicates to aggregate, so a sum of revenue silently becomes an average of revenue.
cells: never silent: that is the point
it hides a grain you did not expect

d.title: A join produces one row per matching pair
d.caption: Two on the left and three on the right for one key is six rows out. This is correct behaviour and it is the mechanism behind every 'my join doubled the revenue' incident. `validate=` makes pandas refuse the join instead of performing it.
cells: 'm:m' is the one to assert against

d.title: value_counts has three defaults, and each changes a number
d.caption: It is a `groupby`-size in disguise: sorted by count descending, with missing values dropped. `normalize=True` computes the share over the **non-missing** rows, so on a column that is 40% missing the proportions sum to 1 over the other 60%.

d.title: Split, apply, combine — and the function decides the shape
d.caption: `.groupby()` computes nothing: it holds the instructions until an aggregation asks for a result. What comes back is decided entirely by what the applied function returns — one value per group, one value per row, or a frame — which is the distinction 4.2 is built on.

d.title: The two arguments that change the row count
d.caption: Both default to a value that produces rows you did not expect. With categorical keys, `observed=False` emits a row for every category **combination**, which on two categoricals is their cartesian product — most of it empty.

d.title: agg collapses, transform does not
d.caption: Every 'compared to its group' feature is a transform: deviation from the group mean, share of the group total, rank within the group. It returns the group statistic with the **original index**, so it drops straight in as a new column with no merge.

d.title: Three kinds of window, and what each includes
d.caption: All three include the **current row**, which is why an unshifted window is a leak: the feature for today already contains today's value. `shift(1)` is what turns a window into a statement about the past.

d.title: Downsampling aggregates; upsampling invents
d.caption: `resample` is a `groupby` whose keys are time bins. Going from hourly to daily combines rows you have. Going from daily to hourly creates bins you have no data for, and every fill method is a decision about what to pretend — which is where data gets invented.

d.title: What the .str accessor costs, and the argument that raises
d.caption: On `object` dtype every `.str` method is a Python loop, one call per element. Arrow-backed strings run the same methods in C. The `na=` row is the one that bites in a filter: `contains` returns `NaN` for a missing input, and a `NaN` inside a boolean mask raises.

d.title: The chain's four verbs
d.caption: Every step returns a new object, so nothing upstream is modified and the chain cannot contain a chained-indexing bug by construction. `assign` with a callable is the piece that makes it work: the function receives the frame **as it is at that point**, so a column added two lines up is available.
